newsitem.title: UK: Mark perks up on French vote, traders wait and see.
newsitem.headline: Mark perks up on French vote, traders wait and see.

text.p: The mark was higher against the French franc and other European currencies in Europe on Monday but the initial currency market reaction to the first round of French parliamentary elections was one of measured caution rather than frantic trading.
French voters gave the Socialist-led coalition an unexpected 4.5 percentage point lead over the ruling centre-right parties at Sunday's poll. The second round of voting is due next Sunday.
The mark gained just over half a centime on the French franc but had backed off overnight highs in early trading.

Traders and analysts said the modest move in the currency reflects two things -- the first round victory is no guarantee of the final result and few currently believe a Socialist government will renege on France's commitment to European monetary union.

"Really and truly this is still just a case of wait and see," said Richard Hill, head of foreign exchange trading at Bank of America in London. "Any worries that are out there are about the potential to derail EMU."
At 1000 GMT, mark/franc was trading at 3.3754/59 compared with 3.3695/00 late Friday and a high overnight at 3.3773.

"The markets will probably still take the view that monetary union will go ahead on time in 1999 and if that's the case then the downside for the French markets will be limited," said Darren Williams, economist at UBS in London.

Holidays in the UK and U.S. today took the sting out of any initial market reaction and the few traders who manned their desks in London, the world's biggest foreign exchange market, reported extremely quiet conditions.

Dealers in Paris said overnight pressure on the franc had eased and there was no obvious sign of the Bank of France buying francs. However, analysts said the central bank would be prepared to intervene covertly on any additional slippage.
"The Bank of France is a master of intervening without showing its hand," Paul Horne, chief international economist at Smith Barney in Paris, told Reuters Financial Television.
Like the ruling coalition, the Socialist party is in favour of France starting European economic and monetary union (EMU) at the planned start date on January 1, 1999.

They have voiced concerns about the need for the post-EMU budgetary Stability Pact, however, and are more vocal in support of a broad-based start to monetary union which would include the likes of Italy and Spain.
The French Communist Party, however, is against the single currency project as currently framed by the Maastricht Treaty and their support may be needed if a left-wing government is to be formed.

The residual market concern is that post-election demands from a left-wing government in France will lead to a watering down of EMU's budgetary discipline and membership and make it more difficult for Germany to justify abandoning the mark.

This view has so far on Monday overridden speculation about a weaker euro, which would boost the dollar against European currencies, and speculation that Italy may start EMU in 1999, which would rally the lira.

The move to marks for safety, albeit in modest amounts, was the only discernible trend. Mark/lira was at 987.55/65 compared with 985.50/80 late Friday and dollar/mark was at 1.6852/57 compared with 1.6925/30.
European Union officials were quick to reinforce the market view that EMU will go ahead regardless of the French vote.

EU Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy said the single currency was "irreversible" and no new conditions would be imposed. Later, he said nobody was considering renegotiating the EMU Stability Pact.
